prompt: Which of these is an incident under the lesson's definition?

choices.text: A planned maintenance window that goes as planned
choices.why: Planned and harmless: not an incident.

choices.text: Card charges failing for shops
choices.why: Right. Unplanned, harming users, needing a coordinated response now.

choices.text: A broken chart on an internal dashboard
choices.why: A bug, not harming the users of the service.

choices.text: A slow test suite in the pipeline
choices.why: Worth fixing, and not urgent harm to users.

prompt: Why does the lesson call a false alarm a success?

choices.text: Because it gives the team practice for free
choices.why: Practice is a side effect; the point is the cost of waiting.

choices.text: Because false alarms are counted as resolved incidents
choices.why: Counting is not the point.

choices.text: Because it proves monitoring works
choices.why: It may have come from a person, not monitoring.

choices.text: Waiting to be sure costs the users more
choices.why: Right. Declaring must be cheap, so people declare early.

prompt: Which make declaring an incident cheap enough that people do it early? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: One command in a chat tool
choices.why: Right. Seconds, not a form.

choices.text: Anybody may declare, including support
choices.why: Right. Whoever sees it first is rarely the owner.

choices.text: A manager's approval before declaring
choices.why: That is exactly what makes people wait.

choices.text: Treating a false alarm as fine
choices.why: Right. Nobody waits to be sure.

prompt: What question does a severity level answer for everybody at once?

choices.text: How much else should stop for this?
choices.why: Right. It decides who is woken, who is told and how often updates go out.

choices.text: Who caused it?
choices.why: Severity is about impact; blame is no part of it.

choices.text: How long will the fix take?
choices.why: Nobody knows that in the first minutes.

choices.text: Which system failed?
choices.why: Often unknown when severity is set.

prompt: Why is severity decided by impact on users rather than by cause?

choices.text: Because causes are always simple
choices.why: They are often complex, and unknown at first.

choices.text: Because users decide the severity
choices.why: The team decides; impact is the criterion.

choices.text: The cause is still unknown then
choices.why: Right. And it keeps the response pointed at the users.

choices.text: Because the DORA metrics require it
choices.why: DORA says nothing about severity scales.

prompt: Match each Billing situation to its severity on the lesson's scale.

pairs.left: payments failing for one card brand
last year's statement export is slow
a typo on the invoice footer

prompt: You are unsure whether an incident is SEV2 or SEV1. What does the lesson say to do?

choices.text: Pick SEV2 and upgrade if it gets worse
choices.why: Under-calling costs the users the time without the right people.

choices.text: Pick the higher level
choices.why: Right. Downgrading costs a few people an evening; upgrading late costs the users.

choices.text: Wait until the cause is known
choices.why: Severity is set before the cause is known.

choices.text: Ask the users to choose
choices.why: The team decides, from impact.

prompt: An incident starts as SEV2 and is raised to SEV1 ten minutes later. What does that say about the first call?

choices.text: It was a mistake to be recorded against the IC
choices.why: Revising as facts arrive is the process working.

choices.text: It should have waited for more data
choices.why: Waiting is the costliest habit in incident response.

choices.text: Severities should never change once set
choices.why: They are revised freely, with the time recorded.

choices.text: Nothing bad; revising is the process working
choices.why: Right. Each revision is recorded with its time.

prompt: What is the one thing the incident commander must not do?

choices.text: Decide the severity
choices.why: That is the IC's job.

choices.text: Assign the other roles
choices.why: That is the IC's first job.

choices.text: Debug
choices.why: Right. The moment the IC opens a terminal, nobody is coordinating.

choices.text: Choose between rolling back and waiting
choices.why: Choosing between options is exactly the IC's role.

prompt: Match each incident role to its job.

pairs.right: writes down what happened, with times

prompt: Where does the Incident Command System come from?

choices.text: Firefighting, in the 1970s
choices.why: Right. Agencies at the same fire could not coordinate.

choices.text: Google's site reliability engineering book
choices.why: The book draws on it; it is decades older.

choices.text: The DORA research programme
choices.why: DORA measures delivery, not incident roles.

choices.text: Military software projects of the 1990s
choices.why: It comes from firefighting.

prompt: Why is the person who knows the affected system best usually not the best incident commander?

choices.text: Experts are poor at making decisions
choices.why: Nothing says so; their expertise is needed elsewhere.

choices.text: Commanders must be managers
choices.why: Anyone trained can command; seniority is not required.

choices.text: The expert caused the incident
choices.why: Cause is unknown, and blame is not the question.

choices.text: That person is needed on the fix
choices.why: Right. Coordinating would take them away from the fix.

prompt: Put the four parts of an incident update in the order the lesson gives.
items: what is happening, in the users' terms

prompt: Why post "no change, still investigating, next update at 18:30"?

choices.text: Because silence is forbidden by law
choices.why: No law; the reason is practical.

choices.text: It stops questions and shows somebody is on it
choices.why: Right. Updates go out on a clock, whether or not anything changed.

choices.text: To fill the timeline for the postmortem
choices.why: The scribe writes the timeline; updates are for people waiting.

choices.text: Because the cause must be given every 30 minutes
choices.why: Updates leave out speculation about cause.

prompt: Why should incident updates to support leave out a guess at the cause?

choices.text: Support is not allowed to know causes
choices.why: It can, once known; the problem is a guess.

choices.text: Causes are confidential
choices.why: Confidentiality is not the reason.

choices.text: A guess becomes what users are told
choices.why: Right. Cause belongs in the postmortem.

choices.text: Updates must be under fifty words
choices.why: Length is not the rule.

prompt: A decision is taken on a video call during an incident. What should happen next?

choices.text: The scribe writes it into the channel
choices.why: Right. Within a minute, so the channel stays the record.

choices.text: Nothing; everybody on the call heard it
choices.why: People not on the call, and the postmortem, need it.

choices.text: It is sent by email to leadership
choices.why: Leadership gets updates from comms; the record is the channel.

choices.text: It waits for the postmortem
choices.why: By then nobody remembers the exact time.

prompt: D047 was deployed at 17:20 and the first call came at 17:38. How many minutes passed before anybody knew?
What did Lia, the support agent, do right at 17:41?

choices.text: She investigated until she was sure of the cause
choices.why: She did not; she asked straight away.

choices.text: She waited for a second case
choices.why: One double charge on a payments product was enough.

choices.text: She refunded the shop herself
choices.why: Refunds came later, as part of the response.

choices.text: She asked the team at once, with evidence
choices.why: Right. The shop's id and both charge ids.

prompt: Service was restored at 18:15. How many minutes was that after the incident was declared at 17:46?
Measured from the declaration, the incident looks about twice as fast as it was. Which lesson's advice does that illustrate?

choices.text: Lesson 2's: quote percentiles, not averages
choices.why: This is about where a clock starts.

choices.text: Lesson 5's: when the restore clock starts
choices.why: Right. Starting at detection hides slow detection.

choices.text: Lesson 9's: count items instead of estimating
choices.why: Unrelated to incident timing.

choices.text: Lesson 12's: leave slack in the plan
choices.why: Slack helps respond, but this is about measurement.

prompt: Every incident gets its own ___, and everything the responders say is said there.
Detection of the double charge came from a customer's phone call. Which lesson takes that up, and how?

choices.text: Lesson 15, by finding who should have noticed
choices.why: Postmortems do not look for culprits.

choices.text: Lesson 16, by lowering the error budget
choices.why: Budgets do not detect anything by themselves.

choices.text: Lesson 18, on which alerts should exist
choices.why: Right. A duplicate charge is a strong candidate for an alert.

choices.text: Lesson 9, by estimating incidents in advance
choices.why: Incidents are not estimated.
